newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy budget vote "difficult", opposition hardens.
newsitem.headline: Italy budget vote "difficult", opposition hardens.

text.p: Italy's opposition said on Monday it would boycott a vote in parliament this week to approve the 1997 budget, raising the stakes in a battle with centre-left Prime Minister Romano Prodi over the crucial austerity package.

Government undersecretary Enrico Micheli said the decision by Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance and the separatist Northern League not to take part in Thursday's vote made things trickier, but the vote should still be valid.
"The situation is not good, it's complicated and difficult...but there are no worries for the quorum," Micheli told reporters in parliament.
Under complicated parliamentary arithmetic, 316 of the 630 seats in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) are required for a basic quorum.
The government, which needs the hardline Communist Refoundation party for a majority in the Chamber, will be safe if all its supporters, who together hold 324 seats, are present.
The vote is scheduled to be the last in the Chamber before the draft budget passes to the Senate, which Prodi controls.

Prodi, who met hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini for talks, said he was still actively trying to seek a compromise solution after the oppposition toughened its stance in the wake of a huge anti-government demonstration in Rome at the weekend.
"The government is open to dialogue," Prodi said. "Berlusconi's comments surprised me a great deal."

Berlusconi, who delivered a stinging attack on tax hikes in the budget before a crowd of some 500,000 on Saturday, told the lower house the government was trying to stifle debate on the 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) package.
"Being put in the position of it being impossible for us to carry out our rights and duties as the opposition, we will not participate in voting on the budget law," he said.

Prodi's 1997 budget, which aims to slash next year's deficit to give Italy a hope of qualifying for a European single currency planned for 1999, contains hugely unpopular tax hikes including a one-off "Euro-tax" whose details remain unclear.

Massimo D'Alema, whose ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) is the biggest in Prodi's coalition government, said the far higher than expected turnout of Saturday's rally appeared to have gone to the opposition's head.
But he held out an olive branch to Berlusconi on Sunday by saying the government would examine "whether it is possible to correct, and where to correct" the draft budget law.
Political commentators said his overture was designed to safeguard talks he has been championing with the Freedom Alliance on how Italy should tackle constitutional reform.

The Freedom Alliance is particularly opposed to special powers contained in the budget bill that would allow the government to set policy on sensitive measures, including tax, without the need to keep going back to parliament for approval.
"We told the government that you cannot think about imposing taxes without discussing these taxes with parliament," Berlusconi said earlier on Monday.

Micheli said the government hoped there was "still room for reasonableness" and that a meeting Prodi had requested with Berlusconi could go ahead. Freedom Alliance leaders were due to meet later on Monday to discuss their position.

Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said the parties with a majority in parliament should press on with approving the budget, saying the special powers Prodi was seeking did not give him a free hand in parliament.
